content: Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP) is a severe lung infection caused by the fungus Pneumocystis jirovecii. It primarily affects individuals with weakened immune systems, such as those with HIV/AIDS, cancer, chronic lung diseases, or those taking immunosuppressive medications like corticosteroids. Without treatment, PCP can be fatal. PCP is transmitted through airborne particles, spreading from person to person. Some healthy adults may carry the Pneumocystis fungus in their lungs without showing symptoms, but they can still transmit it to others, particularly those with compromised immune systems. Symptoms of PCP typically develop gradually over days or weeks and include fever, cough, difficulty breathing, chest pain, chills, and fatigue. These symptoms can become life-threatening if left untreated. Risk factors for PCP include having HIV/AIDS (30–40% of PCP cases occur in this population), undergoing solid organ or stem cell transplantation, having autoimmune or inflammatory diseases like lupus or rheumatoid arthritis, or taking medications that suppress the immune system. There is no vaccine available to prevent PCP. However, prophylactic medications, such as trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (TMP/SMX), are recommended for individuals at high risk, including those living with HIV, transplant recipients, and patients on long-term high-dose corticosteroids. Alternative medications are available for those who cannot tolerate TMP/SMX. To diagnose PCP, healthcare providers may collect a sample of mucus (sputum) from the lungs, perform a lung biopsy, or take a blood sample. Laboratory tests, such as polymerase chain reaction (PCR) to detect Pneumocystis DNA or blood tests for β-D-glucan (a fungal cell wall component), are used to confirm the diagnosis. Treatment for PCP involves prescription medications, with TMP/SMX being the most commonly used. This medication, also known as co-trimoxazole, is administered orally or intravenously for three weeks. Side effects of TMP/SMX may include rash and fever. For patients unable to take TMP/SMX, alternative treatments are available. Unlike most fungal infections, PCP is treated with antibiotics rather than antifungal medications, as antifungals are ineffective against this condition. Historically, PCP was one of the first indicators of the HIV/AIDS epidemic in the 1980s and became a defining illness for AIDS. At that time, approximately 75% of individuals with HIV/AIDS developed PCP. However, the incidence of PCP in people with HIV has significantly decreased due to the widespread use of antiretroviral therapy and prophylactic treatment with TMP/SMX. Despite this progress, PCP remains a common infection in resource-limited settings where access to these treatments is limited. In 2017, there were an estimated 10,590 hospitalizations due to PCP in the United States. However, there is no national surveillance system specifically for PCP in the U.S. Fungal diseases, including PCP, are increasingly recognized as a global health concern, with rising rates of antifungal resistance and frequent misdiagnosis.
